name: Clown contouring

lead: Clown contouring is a makeup technique in which colour correctors, highlighters and contour products are applied in bold, clown-paint-like shapes and then blended into a finished base. YouTuber BellaDeLune popularised it in 2015.

It aims to give stronger definition and brightness than ordinary contouring. Makeup artist Wayne Goss describes it as an exaggerated version of highlighting, contouring and colour correcting, with pinks and fuchsias adding brightness and definition.

paras: Users dab colour-correcting concealer, highlighter and contour in patterned shapes, then blend and blot them into a high-coverage base. Variations include designs such as cat faces or sugar skulls that are blended away.
Described as fun and on-camera rather than an everyday look; one writer who tried it called the result an 'epic disaster'. As with any heavy makeup, skin-sensitivity and removal considerations apply.

Shapes are blended and blotted into the base
angle.text: The shapes are blended into the base so that shadow and light create stronger definition and brightness, mainly visible in photos and on camera.

lead: Clown contouring is a makeup trend that uses colour correctors, highlighters and contour products to paint clown-like designs on the face before blending them into a sculpted finish [1]. YouTuber BellaDeLune is credited with popularising it in a 2015 video; Birchbox reported that it began as a joke, then spread through the hashtag #clowncontouring [1].

Wayne Goss says the technique dates back to the 1960s and describes it as a close relative of highlighting and contouring with added colour, where pinks and fuchsias provide strong colour correction, definition and brightness [2]. Contouring itself has a longer theatrical history: Max Factor added shading to prevent flat faces on film in 1934 [3].

paras: The technique starts with playful shapes in contour and corrector colours that look like clown face paint, then blending turns them into a wearable, high-coverage base [1]. Ordinary contouring places a shade a tone or two darker in the hollows of the cheeks, sides of the nose and temples, with lighter shades on the high points [3].
Birchbox called it more a fun on-camera experiment than an everyday look [1]. Creators have shared before-and-after selfies and variations such as cat faces and sugar skulls [1].

timeline.event: Max Factor adds shading to film makeup to avoid flat faces [3]
